title: Adults outscore preschoolers on creativity tests; the children just enjoy them more
body: On 21 October 2026 psychologists at the University of Graz in Austria, led by Mathias Benedek, [reported in PLOS One](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0346553) a test of the belief that children are more creative than adults. 92 preschoolers and 70 adults, most in their twenties, listed uses for a tin can, drew freely, and drew an animal that doesn’t exist. Five judges who didn’t know anyone’s age rated every idea and drawing from 1 to 5 for novelty, effectiveness and overall creativity, and each person’s tin score was their three best uses, so a long list of ordinary ideas couldn’t win. Adults came out ahead, most clearly in the tasks with a goal. Yet the children felt more confident and motivated, and less anxious about the tin task, and 78.6% of the adults said children are the more creative ones. “Adults don’t lose their creativity, instead they lose the confidence to use it,” Benedek [told the Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2026/oct/21/do-people-become-less-creative-as-they-get-older-research); the study compares two age groups at one moment, so it can’t show how one person changes.

slides.question: In a 2026 study in Austria, what share of the adults said children are more creative than adults?
slides.explanation: 78.6%, nearly four in five. The preschoolers themselves were split: 46.7% said children and 43.5% said adults. Then the judges rated everyone’s work.

slides.alt: Animation on drawing paper in crayon colours: 92 small figures for preschoolers and 70 for adults; a tin can with ideas around it; a house and a fantasy animal; five masked judges, 1 to 5 ratings and a best-three score; tables of who scored higher; tallies of who adults think is more creative.

slides.prompt: Player A lists at least 10 ordinary uses for a tin can, Player B four, mostly original. Find a scoring rule under which B wins.
slides.takeaway: Counting or adding up ratings rewards a long list. Averaging, or taking the best three as the 2026 study did, rewards quality: a weak extra idea doesn’t count against B, and more ordinary ones don’t help A.

slides.heading: How do you measure creativity?
slides.text: A common test asks for as many uses of an everyday object as you can name. Counting answers rewards fast talkers, so the study had five judges rate each idea from 1 to 5 for how new it was and how well it worked, without knowing who had said it, and scored each person by their best three.

left.label: Adults
left.text: Their ideas and drawings were judged newer and more effective, most clearly for the tin can and the fantasy animal.

right.label: Preschoolers
right.text: They felt more confident and motivated, were less anxious with the tin, enjoyed the tasks more, and by their parents’ account create almost every day.

slides.question: In the 2026 Graz study, how was each person’s score for uses of a tin can worked out?
options: The average of their best three
The number of ideas they gave
Their own rating of their work
slides.explanation: Five judges rated each use from 1 to 5, and each person’s score was the average of their three highest-rated uses, so a long list of ordinary ideas could not win on its own.
